back: A genetic change; mutation is the way new alleles are formed.
A random change in the base sequence of DNA.

front: What increases the rate of mutation?
back: Ionising radiation (X-rays, gamma rays, radioactive substances) and some chemicals (for example in tobacco smoke).
notes: UV light damages the DNA of skin cells.

back: Most are harmful or have no effect; a few are useful, such as antibiotic resistance in bacteria.
Only those in gametes (or the cells that make them). Body-cell mutations are not inherited but may cause cancer.
A change in one base of the haemoglobin gene, giving abnormal haemoglobin and sickle-shaped red cells at low oxygen.
notes: Sickle cells block capillaries and carry less oxygen.

back: Having one sickle-cell allele and one normal allele: usually healthy, with some protection against malaria.
Two copies of a recessive allele, so little or no melanin is made.
notes: Protect skin and eyes from strong sunlight.

back: A chromosome mutation: an extra copy of chromosome 21 (47 chromosomes), usually from chromosomes failing to separate in meiosis.
notes: The chance increases with the mother's age.

back: Mutation, meiosis, random mating and random fertilisation.
